executive_summary: The defining thread of today's content is industrial fragility — the accelerating vulnerability of physical infrastructure, manufacturing systems, and industrial economies to catastrophic failure. The breaking news made this viscerally concrete: a paper mill explosion in Washington state killed at least eight people, and a Blue Origin rocket exploded on the launchpad, delivering a sharp setback to commercial space ambitions. These incidents are not isolated accidents but symptoms of a broader structural story reinforced by The Economist's reporting on Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan suffering industrial rot — three of the world's most sophisticated manufacturing economies showing signs of deep systemic decay. Together, these data points form a single urgent argument: the physical and industrial foundations that underpin modern economies and technological ambitions are under severe stress, and the consequences of neglecting them are no longer theoretical. This thread matters because industrial capacity is the hidden substrate of geopolitical power, economic resilience, and technological leadership — and today's content, from mill floors to launchpads to Asian factory corridors, reveals that substrate cracking in real time.

newsletters.title: Well: Getting grandparents and grandkids to connect

items.headline: How to get grandparents and grandkids to connect more often
items.blurb: Experts say it's easy to lapse into superficial or guilt-induced communication between grandparents and grandkids. Kids can think older adults aren't relevant, but grandparents also assume every kid would rather scroll on a device than talk to them. If conversations are easy and fulfilling, they are likely to be more frequent. Tips include letting go of long phone calls, using texts and audio messages, and asking deeper questions to break out of conversation ruts.

newsletters.title: The upset no one saw coming

items.headline: The favorite falls
items.blurb: Jannik Sinner's bid for a career Grand Slam wilted at the French Open in the second round Thursday afternoon. The world No. 1 entered his match with 30 straight wins but lost 3-6, 2-6, 7-5, 6-1, 6-1. Sinner's defeat, to Argentina's world No. 56 Juan Manuel Cerúndolo, was a seismic shock, considering Sinner was once four points from victory.

items.headline: Is tennis ready for what's coming?
items.blurb: Temperatures were around 90 degrees during Sinner's loss, which is not sufficient to engage the French Open's heat rule, a spokesperson for the French Tennis Federation said.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Two industrial and transportation accidents dominated the day's news. A paper mill explosion in Washington state killed at least eight people, with the death toll still rising [2]. Separately, Blue Origin suffered a significant setback when one of its rockets exploded on the launchpad during a test firing [1]. Neither incident involved reported crew casualties in the rocket incident, but both underscore ongoing safety concerns in industrial and aerospace operations. On New York City's streets, a head-on collision between a scooter rider and a cyclist on a city bridge left two people dead [3], adding to a series of traffic fatalities on the city's roadways.

On the media front, CBS made a notable leadership move at its flagship newsmagazine, naming an outsider to take the helm of '60 Minutes' [4]. The appointment signals a potential shift in editorial direction at one of American television's longest-running news programs, which has faced internal turbulence in recent months.
